title: Basic Research Definition - Canadian SR&ED Tax Glossary
description: Learn how Basic Research is defined under Canadian SR&ED tax credit rules in our glossary for businesses conducting scientific investigations.
summary: Basic research is one of three categories of scientific research and experimental development (SR&ED) defined in subsection 248(1) of Canada's Income Tax Act. It covers work undertaken to advance scientific knowledge without a specific practical application in view and, when carried out as a systematic investigation in Canada, can qualify a taxpayer for SR&ED deductions and investment tax credits.

body.text: Basic research is one of three categories of scientific research and experimental development (SR&ED) defined in subsection 248(1) of Canada's Income Tax Act. It covers work undertaken to advance scientific knowledge without a specific practical application in view and, when carried out as a systematic investigation in Canada, can qualify a taxpayer for SR&ED deductions and investment tax credits.
Executive Overview of the Canadian Research and Development Fiscal Landscape

Canada maintains one of the most mature, generous, and legally intricate research and development (R&D) fiscal incentive architectures in the industrialized world. The cornerstone of this federal apparatus is the Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Tax Incentive Program, administered jointly through policy formulation by the Department of Finance Canada and operational enforcement by the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA). Unlike discretionary grants that depend on competitive intake windows, subjective ministerial selection, or finite departmental budget allocations, the SR&ED program is a statutory entitlement embedded directly within the Income Tax Act (R.S.C., 1985, c. 1 (5th Supp.)) and the Income Tax Regulations (C.R.C., c. 945). Any taxpayer carrying on qualifying scientific or technological investigation in Canada that satisfies the statutory criteria of subsection 248(1), section 37, and section 127 of the Income Tax Act is legally entitled to claim both an immediate or indefinitely carry-forwardable income tax deduction and an Investment Tax Credit (ITC).

In fiscal year 2024–2025, the SR&ED program delivered $4.5 billion in investment tax credits across more than 19,000 claimants and over 22,000 processed claims. By the fiscal year ended March 31, 2026, total annual program volume expanded to $4.9 billion in investment tax credits claimed and $4.6 billion allowed across roughly 23,677 to 24,160 processed claims, representing an upward trajectory of approximately 50% in annual credit value delivered since fiscal 2022. At more than $4.5 billion to $4.6 billion annually, the SR&ED program is larger than the National Research Council's Industrial Research Assistance Program (IRAP), CanExport, and the Strategic Innovation Fund combined, serving as Canada's primary non-dilutive capital source for domestic enterprises. Despite widespread industry perception that CRA technical and financial reviews are prohibitively adversarial, empirical program statistics from the most recent reporting cycle demonstrate that 96% of all filed SR&ED claims ultimately result in allowed credits—with 90% of claims accepted exactly as filed, 6% accepted following audit modifications, and only 4% denied in their entirety. Consequently, audit risk in the Canadian SR&ED regime resides overwhelmingly in the quality of contemporaneous documentation and claim preparation rather than in any institutional reluctance by the tax authority to disburse statutory entitlements.

Between 2024 and 2026, the Canadian R&D tax landscape underwent its most consequential structural modernization in over a decade. Following two phases of national stakeholder consultations initiated by the Department of Finance Canada in January 2024 and April 2024, alongside policy announcements in Budget 2024: Fairness for Every Generation, the 2024 Fall Economic Statement, and Budget 2025, Parliament enacted Bill C-15 (Budget 2025 Implementation Act, No. 1) (S.C. 2026, c. 3), which received Royal Assent on March 26, 2026. Taking retroactive statutory effect for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024 (that is, on or after December 16, 2024), Bill C-15 doubled the annual expenditure limit for the enhanced 35% refundable credit from $3 million to $6 million (raising the maximum annual cash refund to $2.1 million), widened the prior-year taxable capital phase-out corridor from $10 million–$50 million to $15 million–$75 million, extended access to the 35% enhanced refundable credit to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) for the first time, introduced an elective gross revenue phase-out calculation for Canadian-Controlled Private Corporations (CCPCs), and restored the SR&ED eligibility of capital expenditures and equipment lease costs after a ten-year hiatus. Concurrently, on April 1, 2026, the CRA launched a formal, elective Pre-Claim Approval Process to provide qualifying businesses with binding upfront technical certainty within eight weeks of application.

body.text: The second- and third-order economic implications of this legislative overhaul are substantial. Under the pre-2025 regime, Canadian technology, biotechnology, and advanced manufacturing firms encountered a severe fiscal cliff upon executing an initial public offering (IPO) on a designated stock exchange or upon scaling their balance sheets past $10 million in taxable capital. Going public automatically stripped a domestic innovator of CCPC status, plunging its federal SR&ED rate from a 35% cash-refundable credit to a 15% non-refundable credit that yielded zero immediate liquidity for pre-profit public issuers. By extending the 35% refundable credit to ECPCs and lifting the taxable capital phase-out floor to $15 million (and ceiling to $75 million), Parliament eliminated the tax penalty against domestic public listings and mid-market capital formation. Simultaneously, the restoration of capital expenditure eligibility directly alters capital allocation mathematics for hardware-intensive sectors—most notably artificial intelligence firms procuring graphic processing unit (GPU) clusters, semiconductor fabricators, clean technology developers, and bio-manufacturers—which were previously disincentivized from purchasing dedicated research apparatus inside Canada following the 2014 repeal of capital expenditure eligibility.
Statutory and Legislative Architecture of the Federal SR&ED Program
Dual-Benefit Structure under the Income Tax Act

The federal SR&ED framework operates through a bifurcated statutory mechanism within the Income Tax Act that separates the deduction of research expenditures from the generation of investment tax credits. These two mechanisms are governed by distinct statutory sections, follow different pooling and carry-forward rules, and interact sequentially across consecutive taxation years.

The first statutory pillar is the SR&ED Expenditure Deduction Pool governed by section 37 of the Income Tax Act. Pursuant to subsection 37(1), a taxpayer carrying on business in Canada may pool all allowable current SR&ED expenditures (paragraph 37(1)(a)) and, for property acquired after December 15, 2024, allowable capital SR&ED expenditures incurred in the taxation year. The taxpayer may deduct any portion of this section 37 pool in the current taxation year to reduce net income for tax purposes, or elect to retain undeducted balances in the pool to be carried forward indefinitely and deducted against taxable income in any future taxation year. This indefinite carry-forward prevents SR&ED deductions from expiring inside standard 20-year non-capital loss carry-forward windows, allowing pre-revenue enterprises to preserve their tax shield until commercial profitability is achieved.

The second statutory pillar is the SR&ED Investment Tax Credit (ITC) governed by section 127 (specifically subsections 127(5) through 127(12.3), with key statutory definitions housed in subsection 127(9)) of the Income Tax Act. While the section 37 pool determines income deductibility, subsection 127(9) defines a claimant's "qualified expenditure" for the purpose of calculating the annual SR&ED ITC. Unlike the section 37 deductible expenditure pool, the SR&ED qualified expenditure pool is calculated exclusively at the end of each individual taxation year and does not carry over as an expenditure pool to subsequent taxation years. Instead, the qualified expenditure pool immediately generates an ITC at either the 35% enhanced rate or the 15% basic rate. To the extent that a claimant's generated ITC is non-refundable and is not utilized to offset federal Part I tax payable in the current taxation year, the unused ITC itself may be carried back 3 taxation years or carried forward 20 taxation years to offset federal Part I tax payable in those years.

Crucially, to prevent double dipping between the section 127 tax credit and the section 37 tax deduction, the Income Tax Act mandates an automatic recapture and pool-reduction mechanism (paragraph 37(1)(e)): any federal SR&ED ITC claimed by a taxpayer in a taxation year (whether refunded in cash or applied to reduce Part I tax payable) reduces the taxpayer's section 37 deductible SR&ED expenditure pool in the immediately following taxation year (or is included directly in taxable income if the section 37 pool balance has already been deducted to zero). Consequently, while the 35% or 15% percentage applies strictly to the investment tax credit rather than the income deduction itself, claiming the credit creates a deferred tax effect in the subsequent fiscal period that must be modelled in corporate T2 tax provisions.
The Definition of SR&ED under Subsection 248(1)

The gateway to both section 37 deductibility and section 127 investment tax credits is the statutory definition of "scientific research and experimental development" codified in subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act. Subsection 248(1) defines SR&ED as a systematic investigation or search that is carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis and that is undertaken in one of three primary categories, supplemented by restricted classes of directly commensurate supporting work. The first category is basic research, which encompasses work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge without a specific practical application in view. The second category is applied research, which encompasses work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge with a specific practical application in view. The third and largest category for commercial claimants is experimental development, which comprises work undertaken for the purpose of achieving technological advancement for the purpose of creating new, or improving existing, materials, devices, products, or processes, including incremental improvements thereto. In addition to these three core categories, subsection 248(1) includes eligible supporting work with respect to engineering, design, operations research, mathematical analysis, computer programming, data collection, testing, or psychological research, but strictly on the condition that such activities are commensurate with the needs, and directly in support, of basic research, applied research, or experimental development undertaken in Canada by or on behalf of the taxpayer.

Simultaneously, subsection 248(1) explicitly excludes commercial, industrial, and routine engineering activities from the definition of SR&ED, even if they involve highly trained scientific or engineering personnel. Statutory exclusions encompass market research or sales promotion; quality control or routine testing of materials, devices, products, or processes; research in the social sciences or the humanities; prospecting, exploring, or drilling for, or producing, minerals, petroleum, or natural gas; the commercial production of a new or improved material, device, or product or the commercial use of a new or improved process; style changes; and routine data collection. In practical audit application, the CRA and the courts rigorously exclude the routine application of known engineering techniques, the customization of third-party software libraries to match client specifications, routine website development, and standard A/B testing devoid of underlying technological uncertainty. Conversely, activities such as architecting a novel data pipeline whose throughput at scale was technologically uncertain at the outset, combining two manufacturing processes in an unvalidated manner, or developing a machine-learning model whose architecture required systematic iterative experimentation to overcome technical constraints squarely qualify as SR&ED. Because the statute focuses exclusively on scientific or technological advancement, the CRA does not judge the commercial success of the project; a project that fails commercially—or even fails technically to achieve its performance targets—still qualifies for SR&ED credits provided it sought to resolve genuine technological uncertainty via systematic investigation.

In August 2021, the CRA archived its legacy Eligibility of Work for SR&ED Investment Tax Credits Policy and replaced it with simplified administrative guidelines structured around Two Requirements—the "Why" and the "How"—derived directly from subsection 248(1), which itself did not change. The "Why" requirement asks whether the work is being conducted for the advancement of scientific knowledge or for the purpose of achieving a technological advancement by overcoming a scientific or technological uncertainty that could not be resolved using generally available scientific or technological knowledge or standard practice. The "How" requirement asks whether the work is being conducted by means of a systematic investigation or search carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis by qualified personnel. Satisfying the "How" requirement requires the generation of a hypothesis (an idea consistent with known facts that serves as a starting point for investigation toward resolving a problem), the testing of that hypothesis through experiment or analysis (allowing the hypothesis to evolve as testing progresses), the formulation of logical conclusions based on empirical results, and the maintenance of contemporaneous evidence generated as the work progresses. Furthermore, the CRA defines an "SR&ED project" as a set of interrelated activities that collectively are necessary in attempting to achieve the specific scientific or technological advancement defined for the project by overcoming scientific or technological uncertainty.
Enacted Legislative Modernization: Bill C-15 and the 2024–2026 Reforms
Legislative Chronology from Budget 2024 to Royal Assent of Bill C-15

The statutory rules governing SR&ED claims for current taxation years reflect a comprehensive, multi-stage legislative reform process that culminated in the spring of 2026. On January 31, 2024, the Department of Finance Canada initiated Phase 1 of its formal public consultation on the SR&ED program, which ran until April 15, 2024. That consultation sought stakeholder input across seven core policy questions: how to keep the SR&ED program effective in supporting R&D-intensive Canadian businesses; what improvements to the statutory definition of SR&ED, eligibility criteria, and program architecture should be considered; how to improve complementarity between SR&ED and Canada's existing suite of direct R&D support programs; how to target assistance more effectively; how to ensure the retention of intellectual property (IP) within Canada so innovative firms remain Canadian-owned and operated; how to streamline administration for entrepreneurs; and how to fund enhancements within the program envelope. Alongside the SR&ED consultation, the Department of Finance Canada also conducted parallel consultations on creating a Canadian patent box regime, which similarly closed on April 15, 2024.

On April 16, 2024, the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance, the Honourable Chrystia Freeland, tabled Budget 2024: Fairness for Every Generation in the House of Commons. Budget 2024 committed $600 million over four years commencing in 2025, with $150 million per year ongoing, to enhance the SR&ED program and launched Phase 2 of the SR&ED consultations through May 27, 2024, focusing specifically on technical reforms and expanding access to the enhanced 35% rate for Canadian public companies. Subsequently, the 2024 Fall Economic Statement (tabled in December 2024, Chapter 2) and Budget 2025 (Canada Strong Budget 2025, Chapter 1) expanded the fiscal commitment and finalized the legislative parameters, raising the proposed enhanced expenditure limit from an interim $4.5 million proposal to $6 million.

On March 26, 2026, Bill C-15 (Budget 2025 Implementation Act, No. 1) received Royal Assent, formally enacting these amendments into the Income Tax Act. The SR&ED enhancements enacted by Bill C-15 are binding statutory law—no longer mere budget proposals—and apply retroactively to taxation years that begin after December 15, 2024 (i.e., taxation years commencing on or after December 16, 2024). For depreciable capital property and equipment lease expenditures, the restored eligibility applies to property acquired and available for use, or lease costs incurred, after December 15, 2024 (that is, on or after December 16, 2024). For taxation years that commenced before December 16, 2024, the legacy pre-Bill C-15 rules continue to govern.
The $6 Million Expenditure Limit and Widened Phase-Out Thresholds

Under Bill C-15, the annual expenditure limit eligible for the enhanced 35% federal SR&ED ITC doubled from $3 million to $6 million for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024. Because the enhanced credit is 100% refundable on current SR&ED expenditures for qualifying claimants, this statutory increase raises the maximum annual federal cash refund available to an eligible corporation (or associated group of corporations) from $1.05 million to $2.1 million. Qualified SR&ED expenditures incurred in excess of the $6 million expenditure limit continue to earn the basic 15% non-refundable federal ITC. The $6 million expenditure limit must be shared among all associated corporations within a corporate group.

Furthermore, Bill C-15 substantially expanded the corporate size thresholds at which the $6 million expenditure limit begins to phase out. Under the legacy rules, a CCPC's $3 million expenditure limit was reduced on a straight-line basis once the prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada of the corporation (and its associated corporate group) exceeded $10 million, becoming completely eliminated at $50 million. Under the enacted Bill C-15 rules, the lower prior-year taxable capital phase-out boundary increased from $10 million to $15 million, and the upper prior-year taxable capital phase-out boundary increased from $50 million to $75 million.

Expressed mathematically, for a qualifying CCPC (that does not elect into the gross revenue test) whose prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada across its associated corporate group lies between $15,000,000 and $75,000,000, the annual $6,000,000 expenditure limit is calculated as:

Expenditure limit = $6,000,000 × ($60,000,000 − A) ÷ $60,000,000, where A is the amount by which the prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada of the corporation and its associated corporations exceeds $15,000,000.

Consequently, every $10 of prior-year taxable capital above $15 million reduces the $6 million expenditure limit by $1, until the enhanced expenditure limit is fully extinguished at $75 million of taxable capital, above which all qualifying expenditures earn the basic 15% non-refundable rate.
Extension of the 35% Refundable Credit to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) and Revenue Election

A foundational reform in Bill C-15 is the extension of the enhanced 35% refundable SR&ED tax credit to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) for taxation years beginning on or after December 16, 2024. Under the Income Tax Act as amended by Bill C-15, an ECPC is defined as a corporation that throughout the taxation year is resident in Canada, has a class of shares listed on a designated stock exchange (or has elected, or been designated by the Minister, to be a public corporation), and is not controlled, directly or indirectly in any manner whatever, by one or more non-resident persons. Corporations controlled by non-residents or foreign parent companies remain ineligible for the 35% enhanced rate and continue to earn the basic 15% non-refundable federal ITC.

Because public corporations often carry substantial book equity that would distort a taxable capital test, an ECPC's $6 million expenditure limit is phased out using a three-year average gross revenue test, where the refundable expenditure limit is gradually phased out as average annual gross revenue over the three preceding fiscal years increases. Crucially, Bill C-15 also permits CCPCs and their associated groups to elect to have their $6 million expenditure limit determined using this exact same gross revenue phase-out structure instead of the $15 million–$75 million prior-year taxable capital test. This election provides vital liquidity relief to capital-intensive private corporations—such as biotechnology, cleantech, energy, and deep-tech hardware startups—that have raised substantial venture capital or debt financing (inflating their taxable capital employed in Canada past $15 million) while remaining pre-revenue or generating modest commercial revenues.
Companion Productivity and Accelerated Capital Cost Allowance (CCA) Measures in Bill C-15

In addition to direct amendments to sections 37 and 127, Bill C-15 enacted companion capital cost allowance (CCA) incentives designed to accelerate R&D and digital infrastructure investment across Canada. Specifically, Bill C-15 provides 100% immediate expensing (a full first-year write-off) for qualifying purchases of depreciable property acquired on or after April 16, 2024, that become available for use before January 1, 2027, across three productivity-critical asset classes: Class 44 (patents or rights to use patented information for a limited or unlimited period), Class 46 (data network infrastructure equipment and related systems software), and Class 50 (general-purpose electronic data-processing equipment, such as computers, servers, and GPUs, and systems software).

Furthermore, Bill C-15 temporarily reinstates the Accelerated Investment Incentive (AII) and immediate expensing for certain qualifying assets, providing an enhanced first-year CCA deduction for eligible property acquired after 2024 and available for use before 2030, with a gradual phase-out starting in 2030 and full elimination after 2033 (replacing the prior rules under which the AII was progressively phasing out between 2024 and 2027). Alongside these enacted Bill C-15 provisions, the federal government has advanced proposed legislation for a broader Productivity Mega Deduction, though Class 1 buildings (including manufacturing and processing buildings) are excluded from the proposed mega deduction and must instead rely on the separate temporary immediate-expensing measure for qualifying manufacturing and processing buildings announced in Budget 2025.
Qualifying Expenditures (QREs) and Calculation Mechanics

To claim SR&ED tax incentives, a taxpayer must first determine its allowable SR&ED expenditures under section 37 (Part 3 of Form T661) and then adjust that figure to arrive at its total qualified SR&ED expenditures for ITC calculation purposes under subsection 127(9) (Part 4 of Form T661).

body.text: Salaries, Wages, and Specified Employee Restrictions

Salaries and wages represent the largest expenditure component of most Canadian SR&ED claims. Eligible salaries are restricted to employees directly engaged in the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada (hands-on experimentation, analysis, and direct technical supervision), alongside employees performing commensurate supporting work under subsection 248(1). Under section 37, salaries and wages for permissible SR&ED work performed outside Canada may be claimed only if the work is performed directly by an employee who is resident in Canada, the remuneration is not subject to an income or profits tax imposed by another country, and the total foreign SR&ED salary claimed does not exceed 10% of the total SR&ED salaries and wages incurred for work performed in Canada. Foreign permissible salaries are excluded from the salary base used to compute the 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount.

Stringent statutory anti-avoidance caps apply to "specified employees"—defined in subsection 248(1) as any employee who does not deal at arm's length with the claimant or who is a specified shareholder owning, directly or indirectly, 10% or more of the issued shares of any class of the capital stock of the claimant corporation or a related corporation. Because most startup founders and owner-managers are specified employees, their compensation is subject to four strict limitations. First, all bonuses, remuneration based on profits, and taxable benefits are strictly excluded from SR&ED claims for specified employees. Second, the maximum deductible and ITC-eligible direct salary for a specified employee is restricted to the lesser of actual non-bonus salary allocated to SR&ED and five times the Year's Maximum Pensionable Earnings (YMPE) determined under the Canada Pension Plan, prorated by the number of days the individual was employed in the taxation year. Thus, claiming an owner-manager's $250,000 salary at face value without applying the specified-employee restrictions is a common filing error that triggers automatic partial disallowance upon CRA review. Third, when calculating the 55% overhead proxy under the proxy method (Part 5 of Form T661), a specified employee's includable salary in the salary base is capped at the lesser of 75% of their total salary and wages (excluding bonuses and taxable benefits) and 2.5 times the YMPE, prorated for the number of days employed in the taxation year. For a calendar 2026 taxation year-end, that 2.5× YMPE ceiling equals $186,500. Fourth, founders and owner-managers who remunerate themselves via dividends rather than T4 payroll employment income generate zero eligible SR&ED salary and add nothing to the proxy overhead salary base.
Overhead Methodologies: Proxy Method vs. Traditional Method

Every SR&ED claimant must elect on Form T661 whether to calculate its SR&ED overhead using the Proxy Method (Line 160) or the Traditional Method (Line 162). Pursuant to subsection 37(10) of the Income Tax Act, this election must be made on the first Form T661 filed for the taxation year and is irrevocable for that taxation year once the form is filed—a claimant cannot subsequently amend its return to switch from the proxy method to the traditional method or vice versa. Consequently, tax practitioners must run parallel calculations under both methodologies prior to initial submission.

Under the Proxy Method (Income Tax Regulations, section 2900), instead of tracking and itemizing specific overhead expenses, the claimant computes a notional Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) equal to 55% of the salary base of employees directly engaged in SR&ED in Canada (reported on Line 502 of Form T661). The PPA is added directly to the claimant's qualified expenditures in Part 4 to earn the 35% or 15% ITC, but it is not an actual cash outlay and is not included in the section 37 deductible expenditure pool (instead, actual overhead expenses remain deductible as ordinary business expenses under the general provisions of the Income Tax Act). Furthermore, the PPA is subject to an overall statutory ceiling: it cannot exceed the total of the corporation's actual eligible overhead-type expenses deducted for the year.

Under the Traditional Method (Income Tax Regulations, paragraph 2900(2)(c)), the claimant enters zero for the PPA and instead itemizes actual overhead and other expenditures on Line 360 of Form T661. To qualify under the traditional method, every claimed overhead cost must be proven to be directly attributable to the prosecution of SR&ED carried on in Canada—meaning it must be both directly related to the SR&ED work and incremental (it would not have been incurred had the SR&ED not occurred). While the proxy method is financially superior and administratively simpler for software, artificial intelligence, and salary-intensive claimants, the traditional method can yield a larger claim for facility-heavy, utility-intensive, or subcontractor-reliant industrial operations where actual incremental shop-floor overhead and sub-90% equipment lease allocations exceed 55% of direct in-house payroll.

To illustrate the exact statutory mechanics of a proxy method calculation under the post-Bill C-15 rules (Form T661 Version 26), consider a qualifying CCPC in calendar year 2026 with $600,000 in eligible SR&ED salaries (yielding a $586,500 PPA salary base after applying the specified employee cap), $75,000 in consumed materials, and $100,000 in arm's-length Canadian subcontractor costs:

body.text: Subcontractors, Non-Arm's-Length Contracts, and Third-Party Payments

When a claimant contracts out eligible SR&ED work to an arm's-length contractor, 100% of the contract expenditure is deductible in the section 37 pool, but subsection 127(9) limits the qualified expenditure for ITC purposes to 80% of the contract expenditure (imposing a mandatory 20% statutory reduction to prevent the claimant from earning ITCs on the contractor's commercial mark-up). Three strict statutory conditions govern subcontractor claims. First, the contracted SR&ED work must be physically carried on in Canada; payments to U.S. or other foreign contractors or offshore software development shops for work performed outside Canada earn 0% SR&ED tax credits. Second, under the CRA's Total Qualified Expenditures for Investment Tax Credit Purposes Policy (Section 9.0), if a current SR&ED contract expenditure is paid or payable to, or for the benefit of, a person or partnership that is not a "taxable supplier", it is completely excluded from the calculation of total qualified SR&ED expenditures for ITC purposes. Third, the contractor must perform eligible SR&ED work on behalf of the claimant, and the contract terms should clearly delineate the technical work performed.

Where SR&ED is subcontracted to a non-arm's-length (NAL) performer (such as a parent, subsidiary, or sister corporation), the expenditure is reported on Line 345 of Form T661. While deductible to the payer under section 37, a NAL contract payment earns no ITC for the payer directly. Instead, the NAL performer incurs the underlying salary and material costs and may either claim the SR&ED ITC on its own return or execute Form T1146 (Agreement to Transfer Qualified Expenditures Incurred in Respect of SR&ED Contracts Between Persons Not Dealing at Arm's Length, updated May 15, 2026) to transfer the qualified expenditures to the payer's qualified expenditure pool. Similarly, non-arm's-length parties use Form T1145 (Agreement to Allocate Assistance for SR&ED Between Persons Not Dealing at Arm's Length, updated May 15, 2026) to allocate government assistance across related entities.

Third-party payments are payments made to an approved university, college, research institute, or other qualifying non-profit R&D organization to conduct SR&ED in Canada that is related to the claimant's class of business. Like arm's-length contracts, third-party payments are included in qualified expenditures at 80% (subject to a 20% reduction in Part 4) and require the claimant to complete and file Form T1263 (Third-Party Payments for Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED)) for each recipient organization.
Restored Capital Expenditures, Shared-Use Equipment (SUE), and Lease Costs

Pursuant to Bill C-15, capital expenditures incurred for depreciable property acquired and available for use after December 15, 2024, and equipment lease costs incurred after December 15, 2024, are once again eligible for both section 37 deductibility and section 127 ITCs. Conversely, expenditures for depreciable property or for the right to use property acquired before December 16, 2024, remain strictly ineligible for SR&ED tax incentives. Under the restored post-December 15, 2024 regime, the statutory rules differentiate based on asset classification, intensity of SR&ED operating usage, and the claimant's elected overhead method.

For All or Substantially All (ASA — ≥90%) Capital Equipment, depreciable capital property (such as laboratory apparatus, specialized manufacturing test rigs, or dedicated AI/ML GPU compute infrastructure) acquired and available for use after December 15, 2024, that is intended to be used all or substantially all (over 90% of its operating time over its useful life) for SR&ED in Canada is 100% includable in the section 37 pool and 100% includable in qualified expenditures for ITC purposes. For a qualifying CCPC claiming the 35% enhanced ITC on capital expenditures within its $6 million expenditure limit, 40% of the resulting 35% ITC is refundable in cash (yielding a 14% immediate cash refund and 21% non-refundable credit on the capital cost), whereas current expenditures are 100% refundable. Under the proxy method, general-purpose office equipment or furniture (GPOEF) is strictly excluded from capital claims.

For Shared-Use Equipment (SUE — >50% to <90% SR&ED Use), depreciable equipment (other than GPOEF) acquired and available for use after December 15, 2024, that is used primarily (more than 50% but less than 90% of its operating time) for SR&ED in Canada qualifies as Shared-Use Equipment on Line 504 of Form T661. Rather than claiming 100% upfront, if the equipment meets the requirements of first-term and second-term SUE, the claimant includes 25% of the capital cost of the equipment in qualified expenditures in the first period (first-term SUE) and the other 25% of the capital cost in the second period (second-term SUE), for a cumulative 50% qualified expenditure inclusion.

For Equipment Lease Expenditures incurred after December 15, 2024, the CRA's updated Lease Expenditures Policy establishes distinct rules depending on whether the claimant elects the traditional method or the proxy method. When a claimant chooses the Traditional Method, if leased equipment is used 90% or more of the time (ASA) for SR&ED in Canada (subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(A)(I)), 100% of the lease expenditure is claimed on Line 350 of Form T661. If leased equipment is used less than 90% of the time in SR&ED after December 15, 2024, the proportional percentage of the lease cost used for SR&ED may still be included in the pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures on Line 360 as overhead and other expenditures, provided the lease expenditure is directly attributable (both directly related and incremental) to the prosecution of SR&ED carried on in Canada under Regulation 2900(2)(c). Conversely, when a claimant chooses the Proxy Method, if leased equipment (other than GPOEF) was used 90% or more of its operating time for SR&ED in Canada (subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(I)), 100% of the lease cost is claimed on Line 350. If leased equipment (other than GPOEF) was used more than 50% ("primarily") but less than 90% of its operating time for SR&ED in Canada (subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(VI)), 50% of the cost to lease the equipment may be claimed on Line 355. Under the proxy method, lease expenditures for equipment used 50% or less of its operating time for SR&ED in Canada cannot be claimed at all. Furthermore, only lease costs for equipment where the performer made the capital expenditure after December 15, 2024, may be included.

Certain categories of expenditures remain permanently excluded by statute or regulation. Expenditures for the acquisition, construction, or lease of a building, or a leasehold interest in a building, are strictly excluded under paragraph 37(8)(d)(ii) of the Income Tax Act. Similarly, unpaid expenditures (subsection 127(26)) (other than salaries and wages) that remain unpaid 180 days after the end of the taxation year are excluded from qualified expenditures in the year incurred; when the claimant subsequently pays the unpaid contract expenditure in a later taxation year (for example, in the 2025 tax year), 80% of the amount paid is entered on the "payment of prior years' unpaid amounts (other than salary or wages)" line of Form T661 for that later year. Finally, SR&ED claim-preparation fees, legal and accounting fees, interest and financing costs, and scientific society dues are prescribed exclusions that earn zero SR&ED ITC (though claim-preparation fees may remain deductible as ordinary business expenses).
Government Assistance, Non-Government Assistance, and Stacking Rules

Pursuant to subsection 127(9), a claimant's qualified SR&ED expenditure pool must be reduced dollar-for-dollar by the amount of any government assistance, non-government assistance, or contract payments in respect of SR&ED that the claimant has received, is entitled to receive, or can reasonably be expected to receive on or before the filing-due date for the taxation year. Direct grants—such as non-repayable contributions from the National Research Council's Industrial Research Assistance Program (IRAP)—and provincial R&D tax credits (such as the Ontario Innovation Tax Credit, the Quebec CRIC, or the BC SR&ED Tax Credit) constitute government assistance that reduces the federal qualified SR&ED expenditure pool.

However, an essential structural mechanic under the proxy method works strongly in the claimant's favour when stacking direct salary grants like IRAP with SR&ED. Because the 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) is calculated in Part 5 of Form T661 on 100% of the gross eligible SR&ED salary base before government assistance is deducted in Part 4, an IRAP grant does not reduce the 55% notional overhead addition. Thus, the claimant retains the full 35% federal SR&ED credit on the 55% PPA generated by the IRAP-funded wages, plus the 35% SR&ED credit on the unsubsidized portion of the wages.
Provincial and Territorial R&D Tax Credit Regimes

Nearly every Canadian province supplements the federal SR&ED program with a provincial R&D tax credit. With the exceptions of Quebec (administered independently by Revenu Québec) and Alberta (administered independently by Alberta Tax and Revenue Administration), provincial R&D tax credits are administered directly by the CRA via supplemental schedules filed with the federal T2 Corporation Income Tax Return, relying on the federal Form T661 technical and financial determinations.

body.text: Ontario: OITC, ORDTC, and OBRITC

Ontario operates a three-tier corporate R&D tax credit system for corporations maintaining a permanent establishment in the province. The primary incentive for small and medium-sized enterprises is the Ontario Innovation Tax Credit (OITC), which provides an 8% refundable tax credit to qualifying CCPCs on eligible Ontario SR&ED expenditures up to an annual expenditure limit of $3 million, yielding a maximum annual cash refund of $240,000 (and a combined federal-Ontario credit rate of up to 43%). Notably, Ontario has not adopted the $6 million federal expenditure limit enacted in Bill C-15, nor has it harmonized its phase-out corridors with the federal $15 million–$75 million thresholds. Consequently, a CCPC's $3 million OITC expenditure limit is progressively reduced when its prior-year federal taxable income lies between $500,000 and $800,000, or when its prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada lies between $25 million and $50 million (both tested across associated corporate groups). To claim the OITC, the corporation must be eligible for the federal ITC under section 127, file federal Form T661, and submit Schedule 566 alongside its T2 return within 18 months of the end of the taxation year (while some informal commentary misidentifies the form as Schedule 552, Schedule 566 is the legally prescribed CRA/Ontario form for the OITC).

Complementing the OITC is the Ontario Research and Development Tax Credit (ORDTC), which provides a 3.5% non-refundable tax credit available to all corporations (both CCPCs and non-CCPCs) on eligible Ontario SR&ED expenditures. Where a CCPC claims both the OITC on Schedule 566 and the ORDTC on Schedule 508, the 8% OITC must first be reconciled and deducted from the qualified Ontario expenditure base before computing the 3.5% ORDTC. Unused ORDTC balances can be carried back 3 taxation years or carried forward 20 taxation years to offset Ontario corporate income tax payable. Additionally, Ontario offers the Ontario Business-Research Institute Tax Credit (OBRITC), a 20% refundable tax credit on qualified contract expenditures incurred under an eligible contract with an eligible Ontario research institute, claimed by filing Schedule 568 and a separate Schedule 569 for each qualifying contract.
Quebec: The Post-March 25, 2025 R&D and Pre-Commercialization Tax Credit (CRIC)

Quebec maintains a fully autonomous corporate tax administration overseen by Revenu Québec. In its 2025–2026 fiscal reforms, Quebec enacted a sweeping structural consolidation of its innovation incentives: for taxation years beginning after March 25, 2025, Quebec replaced its older, fragmented R&D tax credits (including the legacy Crédit d'impôt relatif aux salaires – R-D previously claimed on Form RD-1029.7) with the unified Tax Credit for R&D and Pre-Commercialization (Crédit d'impôt pour la R-D et la précommercialisation — CRIC).

Claimed with Revenu Québec on Form RD-1029.8.CR (with expenditure limit allocation agreements among associated corporations filed on Form RD-1029.7.8), the CRIC is 100% refundable and provides a 30% refundable credit on up to $1 million of eligible expenditures above an exclusion threshold, and a 20% refundable credit on eligible expenditures beyond that $1 million tier (whereas claims made through a partnership earn a flat 20% refundable rate). Critically, unlike the federal SR&ED program—which terminates once technological uncertainty is resolved and strictly excludes commercial product design and certification—Quebec's CRIC covers pre-commercialization work as well as R&D. When combined with the 35% federal SR&ED credit, a qualifying CCPC in Quebec can recover up to 65% of its eligible R&D expenditures in cash refunds.
British Columbia, Alberta, and Prairie Regimes

In British Columbia, the BC SR&ED Tax Credit (BCITC) provides a 10% credit on qualifying BC SR&ED expenditures. In BC Budget 2026, the provincial government made the BC SR&ED tax credit permanent and fully aligned its rules with the federal Bill C-15 expansion. Accordingly, the 10% BC credit is 100% refundable for both CCPCs and Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) up to the $6 million federal expenditure limit (yielding a combined 45% federal-BC refundable rate), and non-refundable for expenditures above the federal limit and for other corporations.

In Alberta, R&D support is delivered through the Alberta Innovation Employment Grant (IEG), administered by Alberta Tax and Revenue Administration (TRA) with the Ministry of Technology and Innovation serving as lead ministry. Delivered through the Alberta corporate tax system on AT1 Schedule 29 without requiring a separate grant application, the IEG applies to eligible R&D expenditures incurred in Alberta after December 31, 2020, that match federal SR&ED eligibility criteria, up to a $4 million annual Alberta spending cap. The IEG provides an 8% refundable payment on eligible Alberta R&D spending up to the corporation's "base level of spending" (calculated as the corporation's average qualifying Alberta R&D spending over the previous two years), and an enhanced 20% refundable payment on eligible Alberta R&D spending that exceeds that two-year average base level. The grant phases out incrementally for firms with between $10 million and $50 million in prior-year taxable capital, and firms with $50 million or more in taxable capital are ineligible (though Alberta has noted it may revisit the grant following the federal Bill C-15 SR&ED changes).

In the Prairie provinces, Manitoba provides a 15% R&D Tax Credit, of which 50% is refundable for internal in-house R&D and 100% is refundable when R&D is conducted under contract with an eligible research institute. Saskatchewan provides a 10% R&D Tax Credit that is refundable for CCPCs on the first $1 million of qualifying annual expenditures and non-refundable above $1 million and for non-CCPCs.
Judicial Precedents, Case Law, and the Common Law Five Questions Test

While the CRA updates its administrative guidance periodically—such as its August 2021 shift from five policy questions to the simplified "Why" and "How" framework—the Federal Court of Appeal has repeatedly ruled that administrative guidelines cannot alter statutory law. Across all Canadian courts, the controlling legal test for whether work satisfies subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act remains the Five Questions Test introduced by Judge Bowman (later Chief Justice of the Tax Court of Canada) in Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Ltd. v. The Queen, [1998] 3 C.T.C. 2520, 98 DTC 1839 (TCC) and formally adopted by the Federal Court of Appeal in C.W. Agencies Inc. v. The Queen, 2001 FCA 393.

body.text: Deep-Dive Analysis of the Five Questions Test

To prevail in a CRA technical review or before the Tax Court of Canada, a claimant bears the legal burden of establishing on a balance of probabilities that each of the five cumulative questions from Northwest Hydraulic and C.W. Agencies is answered in the affirmative.

The first question asks: Was there a technological risk or uncertainty which could not be removed by routine engineering or standard procedures? As established in Northwest Hydraulic and reinforced in RIS-Christie Ltd. v. The Queen and Hypercube Inc. v. The Queen (2015 TCC 65 at para. 48), a project must confront a genuine technical risk or uncertainty that cannot be resolved by known techniques, usual procedures, or standard engineering practice. Uncertainty regarding commercial market acceptance or building a customer-requested feature using standard methodologies does not qualify; the decisive threshold is whether the technical experiment could have failed because the solution was not predictable from publicly available knowledge.

The second question asks: Did the person claiming to be doing SR&ED formulate hypotheses specifically aimed at reducing or eliminating that technological uncertainty? A claimant must articulate specific, testable hypotheses aimed directly at overcoming the identified technological obstacle, rather than engaging in unguided trial and error or ad-hoc parameter adjustments, a distinction that proved decisive in Canafric Inc. v. The King and Clevor Technologies Inc. v. Her Majesty the Queen (2019 TCC 166 at para. 11).

The third question asks: Did the procedure adopted accord with the total discipline of the scientific method including the formulation, testing and modification of the hypotheses? The investigation must follow a systematic, iterative progression of observing constraints, formulating a hypothesis, testing that hypothesis by experiment or analysis, evaluating the empirical results, and modifying the hypothesis across successive iterations.

The fourth question asks: Did the process result in a technological advancement? In Northwest Hydraulic—and as explicitly applied in the 2025 Tax Court of Canada decision in Manning Canning Kitchens Inc. v. His Majesty the King (at para. 27)—Judge Bowman held that this question is answered in the affirmative if the experimental process resulted in an advancement of general scientific or technological understanding, even if the experiment ultimately failed to achieve its commercial or functional goal.

The fifth question asks: Was a detailed record of the hypotheses tested and results kept as the work progressed? As confirmed in Zeuter Development Corporation v. The Queen (2006 TCC 597 at para. 20), documentation must be created contemporaneously as the R&D progresses. Time-tracking logs by project, dated engineering and laboratory notebooks, Git code commit histories, dated meeting minutes, and dated test results all constitute valid contemporaneous evidence, whereas retroactively reconstructed spreadsheets or post-hoc narratives prepared months after fiscal year-end are treated as major audit red flags.
Administrative Filing Procedures, Form T661 (Version 26), and the 2026 Pre-Claim Approval Process
Statutory Filing Deadlines and Prescribed Forms

Under subsection 37(11) of the Income Tax Act and the CRA's SR&ED Filing Requirements Policy, a claimant must file its prescribed SR&ED forms—Form T661 and Schedule 31 (Form T2SCH31) for corporations—no later than 12 months after the claimant's income tax return filing-due date for the taxation year in which the expenditures were incurred. Because a corporate T2 return is due 6 months after the end of the corporation's fiscal year, a corporation's absolute statutory SR&ED reporting deadline is 18 months after its fiscal year-end. For example, a corporation with a December 31, 2025 fiscal year-end has a T2 filing due date of June 30, 2026, and a final SR&ED reporting deadline of June 30, 2027 (similarly, a December 31, 2024 year-end must file by June 30, 2026; a June 30, 2025 year-end by December 31, 2026; and a July 31, 2025 year-end by January 31, 2027). Beyond this 18-month deadline, the claim is statute-barred with zero extensions permitted; if the CRA contacts a claimant regarding an incomplete claim, any missing prescribed information must be submitted before the 18-month reporting deadline or the SR&ED expenditures and related ITC are permanently forfeited.

For a partnership, the partnership itself must file a single Form T661 reporting all of its SR&ED expenditures, rather than one partner's share, and individual partners cannot add partnership SR&ED costs to their own corporate SR&ED expenditure pools. Because a partnership is not a corporation, the SR&ED credit flows through to the partners, and the applicable credit rate is determined at the partner level.

body.text: In Part 2 of Form T661, each claimed project must be described within strict word limits on Lines 242, 244, and 246, capped at 350 words, 700 words, and 350 words, respectively (per Guide T4088). Because the CRA evaluates technological uncertainty rather than business value, these technical narratives should be authored with direct input from the senior engineers and scientists who performed the work rather than marketing personnel.
The New Elective Pre-Claim Approval Process (Launched April 1, 2026)

Announced in the Canada Strong Budget 2025 and officially launched by the CRA on April 1, 2026, the Pre-Claim Approval Process is an optional upfront technical certification pathway that enables eligible businesses to find out whether their R&D projects qualify for SR&ED tax incentives before they begin work or incur any costs. To focus support on startups and small-to-mid-sized enterprises, pre-claim approval is available to businesses that are Canadian-controlled private corporations (CCPCs), Canadian corporations, or Canadian partnerships, have an annual gross income of less than $25 million, and are in good standing with the CRA.

The Pre-Claim Approval Process operates through a structured four-step workflow. First, the business opens a pre-claim approval request by completing a web form that takes less than five minutes and receives a CRA case number within two to five business days. Second, the business completes its streamlined application inside the CRA My Business Account portal in a few hours using existing internal project documentation, requesting pre-claim approval for up to three projects. Third, within four weeks of submitting the application, the business meets with a CRA SR&ED specialist to establish a direct relationship and review the planned work; this meeting is mandatory for new SR&ED claimants and optional at the CRA's discretion for established claimants in good standing. Fourth, within eight weeks of completing the application in My Business Account, the business receives an official pre-claim approval determination from the CRA. If granted, pre-claim approval remains valid for up to three years, and if a subsequent SR&ED claim containing pre-approved projects requires an expenditure review, the CRA's processing time standard is cut in half from 180 calendar days to 90 calendar days.
CRA Service Standards, FTCAS, and Audit Dispute Resolution

The CRA maintains three published processing service standards for refundable SR&ED claims (targeting 90% compliance, whereas non-refundable claims carry no formal processing timeframe standard). First, refundable claims that are accepted as filed are processed within 60 calendar days of the CRA receiving a complete claim and income tax return. Second, refundable claims that are selected for review and only include projects granted pre-claim approval are processed within 90 calendar days. Third, standard refundable claims selected for technical and/or financial review are completed within 180 calendar days.

If a claimant is submitting its first SR&ED claim—or has not submitted an SR&ED claim in the preceding three years—and the CRA's risk assessment identifies the claim as low risk, the claimant may be selected for the First-Time Claimant Advisory Service (FTCAS), a mandatory educational service introduced publicly on January 1, 2014. Conducted by a CRA Research and Technology Advisor and a Financial Reviewer over a one-to-two-hour meeting, FTCAS is not a review or audit of the filed claim: no determinations of work eligibility or expenditure adjustments are made for that year, and the expected refund is released after the meeting. Instead, FTCAS provides tailored guidance on how to identify eligible work, track allowable expenditures, maintain contemporaneous evidence, and file compliant future claims, though the reviewers' notes can influence whether subsequent years' claims are selected for audit.

When a claim is selected for a formal CRA Review (governed by The SR&ED Review Process: A Guide for Claimants, updated in 2026—which superseded the legacy Claim Review Manual for Research and Technology Advisors), CRA reviewers may conduct a desktop review, a financial-only review, or a combined technical and financial review involving virtual or on-site interviews with senior technical and financial personnel. If a claimant has concerns during a review, it should first address them with the assigned Research and Technology Advisor (RTA) and/or Financial Reviewer (FR), and if unresolved, escalate to the Research and Technology Manager and/or Financial Review Manager under the Guidelines for Resolving Claimants' SR&ED Concerns. If the claimant disagrees with the final Notice of Assessment or Reassessment, it has the statutory right to file a formal Notice of Objection within 90 days of the date of the Notice, and if the objection is denied by the CRA Appeals Branch, to file an appeal to the Tax Court of Canada.
Complementary Federal Innovation Grants and Clean Economy Investment Tax Credits

Sophisticated R&D tax planning in Canada requires coordinating SR&ED claims with federal direct funding programs and the newly enacted Clean Economy Investment Tax Credits. Since 2016, the federal government has committed over $16 billion to scientific discovery and research talent, including the $2 billion Global Innovation Clusters, the $3.5 billion Sustainable Canadian Agricultural Partnership (running through 2028), $14.5 million over two years in Budget 2024 for Innovation, Science and Economic Development Canada's (ISED) Innovation Asset Collective to assist SMEs with IP creation and retention, and amendments to the Red Tape Reduction Act to broaden regulatory sandboxes for testing novel products. In Budget 2024, the government also proposed $2.4 billion for artificial intelligence, comprising $2 billion for the AI Compute Access Fund and Canadian AI Sovereign Compute Strategy, $200 million via Regional Development Agencies to accelerate AI commercialization, $100 million for the NRC AI Assist Program for SMEs, and $50 million for workforce transition and the AI Safety Institute of Canada.

Alongside SR&ED, Parliament enacted a comprehensive suite of refundable Clean Economy Investment Tax Credits through Bill C-59 and expanded them significantly in Bill C-15. The Clean Technology Manufacturing ITC provides a 30% refundable tax credit for investments in eligible depreciable property used all or substantially all (≥90%) for clean technology manufacturing or qualifying critical mineral activities (producing copper, nickel, cobalt, lithium, graphite, and rare earth elements). Bill C-15 and Budget 2024 expanded the list of critical minerals and modified the rules for polymetallic projects so that eligible property at mine or well sites (including tailing ponds, mills, smelters, or refineries) qualifies if 50% or more of the financial value of the output comes from qualifying critical minerals, supported by an attestation from an arm's-length qualified engineer or geoscientist and protected by a five-year average mineral price safe harbour rule against ITC recapture. Furthermore, Bill C-15 implemented the Clean Electricity ITC (extending eligibility to provincial and territorial Crown corporations committing to a net-zero grid by 2035 and to the Canada Infrastructure Bank and Canada Growth Fund), extended the full Carbon Capture, Utilization, and Storage (CCUS) ITC rates to the end of 2035 (from the end of 2030, with lower rates applying from 2036 to 2040), expanded the Clean Technology ITC to cover electricity and heat generation from waste biomass and modified rules for small nuclear energy property, expanded the Critical Mineral Exploration Tax Credit, and extended the Mineral Exploration Tax Credit (METC) for flow-through share investors to March 31, 2027.
Strategic Conclusions and Audit Readiness Imperatives

The enactment of Bill C-15 on March 26, 2026, and the launch of the CRA Pre-Claim Approval Process on April 1, 2026, mark a decisive structural expansion of Canadian R&D tax law. By doubling the 35% enhanced refundable expenditure limit to $6 million (for a $2.1 million maximum annual cash refund), widening the taxable capital phase-out corridor to $15 million–$75 million, extending the 35% refundable credit to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs), permitting CCPCs to elect into the three-year average gross revenue phase-out test, and restoring capital expenditure and equipment lease eligibility after December 15, 2024, Parliament has transformed SR&ED into a comprehensive capital formation engine for both emerging startups and scaling mid-market and public enterprises.

To capture the full financial benefit of these enacted reforms while mitigating audit adjustments, Canadian enterprises and their tax advisors should execute five integrated compliance strategies. First, accounting teams must immediately segregate capital equipment acquisitions and equipment lease costs incurred after December 15, 2024, tracking operating time usage to substantiate ≥90% ASA capital claims (100% eligible, 40% refundable at the 35% CCPC rate), >50%–<90% Shared-Use Equipment claims (Line 504: 25% first-term and 25% second-term SUE), and post-December 15, 2024 equipment lease claims across Lines 350, 355, and 360 of Form T661 Version 26, while coordinating Class 44, Class 46, and Class 50 immediate CCA expensing. Second, venture-backed CCPCs whose prior-year taxable capital exceeds $15 million must model whether electing into the newly enacted gross revenue phase-out structure under Bill C-15 preserves a higher $6 million expenditure limit than the $15 million–$75 million taxable capital test, while performing parallel simulations of the irrevocable Line 160 Proxy Method versus Line 162 Traditional Method election before filing Form T661. Third, enterprises operating in Quebec with taxation years commencing after March 25, 2025, must expand their internal project tracking to capture newly eligible pre-commercialization expenditures alongside core R&D on Revenu Québec Form RD-1029.8.CR under the 30%/20% refundable CRIC regime. Fourth, eligible corporations with under $25 million in annual gross income launching multi-year R&D projects should apply for the CRA Pre-Claim Approval Process via My Business Account prior to commencing work, securing up to three years of upfront technical certainty and halving any subsequent expenditure review timeline from 180 days to 90 days. Finally, because the Tax Court of Canada's jurisprudence from Northwest Hydraulic and Zeuter Development through Manning Canning Kitchens confirms that contemporaneous evidence of hypothesis formulation and systematic testing is the decisive factor in defending SR&ED claims, technical leads must embed hypothesis-test-result documentation directly into daily engineering workflows throughout the fiscal year.
